olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: (a) Do there exist 14 consecutive positive integers each divisible by a prime $p$ with $2\leq p\leq 11$? (b) Same for 21 consecutive integers and primes $\leq 13$?
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 1986

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: During a lecture, each of five mathematicians fell asleep exactly twice. For each pair, there was a moment when both were asleep. Prove at some moment three were asleep simultaneously.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 1986

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Find the smallest integer $n>1$ for which the root-mean-square of the first $n$ positive integers is an integer.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 1986

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: Two circles $K_1,K_2$ intersect at $A,B$ with $AB$ a diameter of $K_1$. Point $P$ on $K_2$ is inside $K_1$. Using only a T-square, construct $C,D$ on $K_1$ such that $CD\perp AB$ and $\angle CPD=90^\circ$.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 1986

olympiad_full_name: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad
statement: For partitions $\pi$ of $n$, let $A(\pi)$ = number of 1s in $\pi$ and $B(\pi)$ = number of distinct integers in $\pi$. Prove $\sum_\pi A(\pi)=\sum_\pi B(\pi)$ over all partitions of $n$.
source: United States of America Mathematical Olympiad 1986
